subject: axolotl
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: axolotl with frilly pink gills.
Style: chibi.
reasoning:
I'm planning the chibi axolotl's proportions, going with an exaggerated big-headed style and a body length around 0.28 meters, oriented facing +Z.

I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy: a hips root joint connecting spine, tail, neck/head, jaw, gill joints, and four legs with appropriate toe counts (4 front, 5 hind). I'm sketching out the body silhouette by defining a curve of points from tail tip through hips toward the head to guide the sweep geometry.

Still writing sweep geometry...

For the fin's thickness axis, I'm figuring out the cross product gives centered geometry. Rather than one long bone-bound membrane that wouldn't flex naturally with the tail, I'll split the fin into three separate extrudes, one per tail segment, so each piece binds to its nearest joint.

Actually, I realize membrane is the better tool here—building the fin from two sweep paths (a low edge hugging the skin and a raised offset edge) bound to the tail chain bone, following the documented pattern for attaching membranes to a skeletal path.

I'll simplify to a single chain approach instead: a root "hips" joint at the body's closest point, then a forward "spine" chain and backward "tail" chain both parented to hips, splitting the body curve at that root position following the doc's example pattern.

Reversing the tail slice direction, I'll let joint names default to auto-generated labels like tail1-5 and spine1-3, and add a "head" joint parented to the end of the spine chain, aimed outward at the neck point.

For the jaw I'm adding another joint parented off the head. Thinking about the head geometry now — going chibi-style with a big round scaled sphere, oversized shiny eyes set wide on top/sides like an axolotl but exaggerated, using decals for the eye details, with rough dimensions around 0.17 wide by 0.085 tall by 0.12 long, positioned forward of the neck joint.

I'm adjusting proportions so the tail isn't too long relative to the chibi body, shortening it and compressing the overall body length closer to real axolotl scale while keeping things floor-aligned by height, and planning to add upward-splaying gills that push the total height higher.

For the head, I'm splitting it into a separate upper skull and lower jaw ellipsoid instead of one solid sphere, since a full sphere won't give the mouth opening I want -- building the upper half as a flattened ellipsoid and placing a smaller jaw piece beneath it on its own bone, overlapping slightly, then adding a curved smile line as a decal for the mouth.

Decal vertices would inherit the skin weights of whatever bone they land on, which complicates splitting across jaw and head — simpler to just attach the smile decal to the upper head bone alone, positioned slightly below center on the front face.

I'll skip adding a separate dark mouth-cavity part for simplicity, keeping just the decal. For eyes, I'm placing them at wide azimuth angles on the upper-front of the head, giving that classic axolotl look of eyes facing up and forward on a flat wide head.

I'll settle on elevation 25 with the default up vector for orienting the decal. For the eye itself, I'm considering adding a slightly raised dome in a lighter head color at the hit point, then decaling the eye texture onto that bump surface to give it some dimensionality.

Actually, I'll simplify and skip the bump entirely, decaling a large eye (chibi-style, radius ~0.05) directly onto the head with an eyelid ring outline for definition. I'll also add blush decals below the eyes as soft pink ellipses with hatch lines, plus tiny dark nostril decals or small embedded spheres on the snout.

Now for the gills, the key signature feature: three stalks per side curving up and outward from behind the eyes, each built as a chain of two joints with frilly feather-textured card filaments and a ring of cards along the stalk. I'm deciding between "fan" and "tentacle" as the role for these gill chains, leaning toward "fan", and laying out their base positions around the back sides of the head.

I'm figuring out the fanning directions for the three stalks (up-back, outward-up, outward-down-back), their curved sweep paths with tapering radius, and a pink-red stalk color with gradient feather-textured cards for the filaments, generating outward-facing card frames along each sweep to create the frilly plume effect.

Still writing filament flow logic...

I'll skip tinting and instead bake a root-to-tip color gradient directly into the frond texture itself, going from a deep pink-red at the base to pale pink at the tip, with a tapered leaf shape, dark stroke outline, center vein, and tiny side serrations at 128px size. Stalk tips should carry that same base-to-tip pink banding.

For part counts, each stalk contributes roughly 16 gill cards plus tip fan cards, and with six stalks that's around 100 cards sharing one texture mesh, so triangle counts stay manageable even with extra bend. Rather than forcing a hard 180-340 part target, I'll aim for something like 100-200 parts using a small set of distinct textures -- eyes, blush, smile, filament, body speckle paint, belly marks -- and build out from there.

I'm sketching the body coloring: a countershaded pink coat with speckled spots on the dorsal side fading to a creamy belly, mimicking a leucistic axolotl, with a custom paint function to warm the top and cool the underside for form lighting.

Shading the coat with cool lavender tones below and warm cream tones above...

I'm reusing the coat paint for the head with slight darkening at the top, then considering adding a thin dorsal fin membrane running along the back and tail in deep pink, mindful of edge artifacts if I extrude it as a flat shape.

Still writing extrude logic...

I could try splitting bones between tail and spine sections, but since my membrane's second edge is a custom point-built path rather than a sweep.line, it won't inherit bone cuts automatically the way the surface edge does.

I should also add a ventral fin along the tail's underside, mirroring the dorsal one but offset downward, sampling both edges consistently along arc length. For the fin membrane's coloring, I'm thinking of a gradient that shifts from skin tone near the body to a deeper pink at the outer edge, with subtle ray-like stripes running across it.

Now moving to the legs — axolotls have short stubby limbs with thin digits (four front, five hind), so for this chibi style I want chunky legs with tiny finger nubs. I'm setting up the front legs to splay outward from the shoulder with a bent elbow pointing backward, defining root and target positions along with segment lengths for a simple two-bone limb system.

For leg radius I'll use roughly 0.011, and with three named joints (shoulder, elbow, hand) the chain naturally forms two spans plus a tip joint at the end.

I'll parent the arm to the nearest joint on the front spine chain, using a nearestJoint lookup to find where the shoulder attaches. For sweeping the limb geometry, I'll pick a simple paint color for the limb surface rather than the belly-specific coat.

For hands I'm planning a small flattened palm sphere plus four finger chains per hand, each finger made of two joints (three points), and similarly five-toed chains for the hind feet — keeping joint counts modest (roughly 36 for digits, 18 for gill stalks) so the total stays well under the joint budget.

Now I'm working out the geometry for how each finger fans out from the hand tip, computing world-space positions for the base, middle, and tip joints based on angle offsets and a slight droop toward the floor, with tapering radii for a natural rounded look.

For color, I'm giving the fingertips a paler skin tone than the rest of the digit using a simple threshold function, and I'm figuring out how to structure the finger chain with named joints so the sweep renders three points (base, mid, tip) correctly.

I'm working through the hind leg geometry now - setting hip position, foot target, segment lengths, and knee direction so the IK chain produces a natural bend outward and forward.

Now I need a toe-fan helper for the feet, spreading five digits at roughly 45° around a center direction, and a body radius function that tapers smoothly from a thin, laterally-compressed tail to a wider chest/belly before narrowing toward the neck.

I'll compute the radii by sampling z-depth along the body path rather than raw parameter t, mapping specific z-values to width/height pairs and interpolating smoothly between them with smoothstep easing.

I need the lowest points to actually touch the floor at y=0, with a small tolerance of maybe 2% of body height. So I'm adjusting the chest, tail, and leg coordinates so each y-minus-radius value lands right at zero rather than slightly above it.

Defining profile function...

Now I'm working out the head attachment: head center around z=0.115 with ellipsoid dimensions sized for a chibi proportion, bigger relative to the body. I'm placing the upper head sphere centered near y=0.046 with the jaw overlapping below to hide the seam.

I'm checking the jaw ellipsoid's position and radii against the head so it sits as a cute underbite poking slightly past the upper head's front edge, adjusting its depth to keep it subtle rather than exaggerated.

For the smile, I'm placing a decal on the head near the lower-front area so it reads as a wide, upturned chibi smile sitting just above the jaw seam, even though the two shapes create a slight crease where they meet — which actually works fine visually. Now I'm moving on to positioning the eyes.

Setting head center coordinates, then computing eye placement using azimuth and elevation angles around the ellipsoid to find where the eyes intersect the head's surface...

I realize the direction vector doesn't need to match the surface normal exactly—it's just the facing direction for the decal, so I'm flattening it toward front-facing instead of using the steep elevation. I'm recalculating with elevation 12, azimuth 36 to get a gentler projection that won't stretch the eye decals as much on the curved surface.

Mapping out eye position near x=.04, y=.06, z=.17 with wide spacing around .08, checking the local surface normal there to orient the decal properly, and sizing eyes around 0.05. I'm also placing blush marks below and outside the eyes, and starting to think through the eye texture itself—a dark navy circle with a bright highlight.

Writing eye SVG code...

Adding tiny nostril spheres, a solid pink blush ellipse with darker hatch lines, and small gill-base bumps near the collar in deeper pink for extra head detail.

Placing gill bases using azimuth/elevation hits around the head, then sprouting each stalk as a small appendage chain following a catmull curve from base to tip, with joints spaced along the path.

Still defining stalk offsets...

Going with a deep pink tone for the gill color. For filaments, I'm planning to place small card shapes along the stalk sweep using parametric frames, with rings of four cards at each height step, angled outward and leaning toward the flow direction -- giving roughly 168 cards total across the stalks for that frilly gill texture.

I'm grouping these cards into three size tiers by height (base, mid, tip), each with its own taper range, plus an extra tip fan -- about 18 mesh parts across six stalks, which keeps things manageable since parts are cheap to add.

For orientation, each card's flow direction will just follow the sweep curve's tangent at that point, cast loosely since the frame types don't matter here. I'll add slight random spin variation to the ring angles (0/90/180/270) using a seeded rng so the frills don't look perfectly uniform.

Now I'm sketching the frill texture itself -- a tapered leaf shape with a rounded tip and a slight cusp at the base, drawn as a curved SVG path filled with a gradient.

I'm adding a central vein line down the leaf and setting up a bottom-to-top color gradient from deep pink to pale pink with a darker outline stroke, sized for a 128px icon -- confirming each SVG can safely reuse the same gradient id since they're rendered independently.

I'm also planning small gill-base bumps on the flanks for extra chibi detail, then moving into a helper function for generating hand/finger geometry -- computing each finger's position by spreading them evenly around a center angle based on joint, base vector, direction, count, spread, length, and radius.

I'm working out the finger joint positions and radii so fingertips taper down near the floor without clipping through it, then sizing the palm as a flattened sphere attached to the wrist joint, and finishing with small pale pink bead spheres at each fingertip for a soft rounded look.

Now I'm setting up the finger sweeps with a color function to split each into two segments for base and tip coloring, then moving on to the legs, defining a tapering radius function along the chain for a coat-colored sweep.

For the shoulders, I'm adding a small bump sphere skinned onto the bone for a chunkier look, giving hind legs five toes, and skipping interior mouth detail. I'm also considering a lighter paint under the chin to add subtle shading contrast to the head.

For the muzzle, I'm deciding whether to layer a paint function on top of COAT to lighten the front region or just reuse COAT directly for the head, with the jaw using a separate pale pink tone for a countershaded effect.

Now I'm adding small deep-pink sphere bumps as gill collar details, stuck onto the head bone at each hit point with slight embedding. For pose, I'm keeping the tail straight rather than curved for this chibi rest pose.

I'm designing the dorsal and tail fin as a continuous membrane running along the spine and tail, planning a reusable fin-strip function that samples the bone chain and builds height-varying geometry across it.

Still mapping out fin heights along the body...

I'm sampling points along the sliced bone segments to build the fin edge, then defining the membrane's coloring with a paint function that shifts between pink tones and adds subtle ray-like stripes across the fin surface.

I'm also sorting out naming conflicts—renaming the sweep object from `body` to `trunk` with a `spinePath`—and planning the build order: construct joints and chains first (core, front, back, head), then layer the sweeps on top, with spine chains parented to the core joint.

Then I'm working through the leg and tail attachments: tail chain gets five segments parented to core, hind legs attach to the hips joint, and front legs find their nearest joint near the shoulder using a nearest-joint lookup. For the head, I'm placing it at the neck point along the spine path, parented to the front chain.

Adding the jaw joint next, then shaping the head as a low-poly sphere with non-uniform scaling for the chibi look, deciding to keep it smooth rather than faceted for a cuter appearance.

For eyes, I'm placing decals on the head surface using hit points and directional offsets, mirroring them for symmetry.

For the smile, I'm computing a hit point lower on the face and placing an elongated decal there for the mouth shape.

Then I'm positioning symmetric blush decals at mirrored angles on the cheeks with a slanted texture pattern, adding nostril sticks, a pale jaw bone, and bigger freckle spots on the back, while skipping extras like mouth lining and a tongue to keep things simple. I'm also keeping an eye on the total flat color count to stay within a reasonable palette limit.

Now I'm setting up the imports for the build, carefully only pulling in functions I know exist in the builder library like createBuilder, rng, catmull, limb, paint, spots, mottle, countershade, mix, smoothstep, resolve, and svg, while skipping uncertain ones like frame and aim. Writing profile function...

Checking the leg segment lengths against the hip-to-foot and shoulder-to-hand distances confirms both front and hind limbs fit proportionally given the two-segment lengths I'm using.

Working out the elbow bend direction as a plane preference relative to root and target, then wiring up naming conventions for left/right joints and setting up the sweep call with tapered radii for the limb geometry.

Now I'm writing a helper function to generate finger digits, computing each finger's angle and spread from a center direction, then building joint points along each digit at a fixed height offset.

Working out finger taper radii and colors, then moving on to the palm sphere placement and scale, and the dorsal fin attachment to the bone structure.

Now I'm writing the gill generation logic, sweeping around the head surface on both sides to find attachment points, then building each gill as a sprouted fan shape with base, mid, and tip control points for a smooth curve.

Still computing sweep frames...

The card sits flat perpendicular to the tangent, so leaning it 55° toward the flow makes it flare out like bottlebrush bristles. Since a thin card viewed edge-on from some angles won't read well, I'll enable `cross: true` to add a second card at a right angle so the fronds stay visible from any viewpoint.

Rough triangle budget: with cross enabled and a handful of angles per level across 6 stalks × 8 levels, I'm landing around 6k triangles total, which is manageable, so I'll pick 3-4 angles per level rather than overdoing it. The flow direction is just the tangent of the stalk curve (perpendicular to its normal), so I can use that directly for orienting each card before applying the bend.

For texturing I want two frond variants—a pink FRILL_A and a paler pink-white-tipped FRILL_B—picked randomly per card, giving roughly 36 mesh parts across the calls. Now I'm sketching out a fin/membrane helper that samples points along a path, offsets them vertically by a height function times a sign, builds a Catmull-Rom curve through those offset points, and feeds it into a membrane-generation call with color and thickness settings.

I'm working through whether Path supports slicing for pulling knot ranges, and mapping out the t-ranges for dorsal, ventral, and tail fins based on where the spine and tail bones cross specific z-depths—confirming the dorsal line corresponds to the top-facing side of the tube and figuring out the right closestT lookups for ventral fin boundaries.

The tail fin needs nonzero height even near the tip, and I'm checking that fin membranes stay embedded within the thin tail radius without poking out. I'm also finalizing skin color hex values, confirming freckle placement on the body, and deciding to skip extra details like cheek folds or forehead marks, keeping the pose at rest with no additional bone adjustments before a final API consistency check.

I'm verifying API usage details: surface centers take Vector3 points, path slicing and closest-point lookups accept Vector3 inputs, and the hips joint serves as the root without needing an explicit role. I'm also deciding whether forelimbs should use the "leg" or "arm" chain type for a quadruped like the axolotl, leaning toward "arm" for front limbs per standard rigging convention.

Checking leg chain contact points and polyline input, confirming the root joint placement sits inside the body so the leg sweep base stays hidden under the body radius.

Now I'm defining the hip root point along the spine with its exact z-coordinate, making sure that point is included in the spine path array so the closest-point lookup resolves accurately. Writing the profile lookup function...

Checking the overlap between body end and head start—at z=.07 the body cap is round with small radii, and the head ellipsoid spans roughly ±.068 in x at that same point, so the transition should stay hidden inside the head geometry.

Head top at .088 with gills extending the chibi profile to .15 total. Now I'm checking the jaw hinge placement and verifying the jaw sits correctly tucked under the head's front lower curve without poking through.

Working through the overlap, the jaw's front edge extends just slightly past the head surface, which actually reads as a natural upper-lip overhang. I'm also noticing the smile decal's elevation angle lines up almost exactly with the jaw's top surface height, which should make the mouth placement look coherent rather than floating or misaligned.

Trying a smaller elevation angle of -12 gives a better fit, placing the smile center around y .032, z .177, which sits nicely on the head curve even though the curve dips lower mid-smile and rises at the corners. The blush position at az 55, el -5 checks out fine too, and now I'm working out the eye placement at az 36, el 12, sizing them to span roughly y .035 to .085 on the front surface.

Checking whether the eye at that position overlaps the head's top edge where the surface curves away — recalculating with az 38, el 5 gives a slightly better fit at around (.045, .052, .171), keeping the eye within the front surface rather than stretching over the tilted edge.

To make the eyes read better as round chibi eyes, I'm thinking of adding a small protruding bulb — a glossy pink sphere around radius .021 embedded halfway into the head — then decaling the eye texture onto that bulb surface at size .036 for a more convincing 3D eye.

I'll place the bulb half-buried at the head surface, with the eye decal projected outward on its front face sized to cover it, positioning eyes symmetrically near the top. I'm also setting up a blush decal on the skin and planning out five total textures: eye, smile, blush, and two frills.

Writing SVG code...

Adding small highlight details...

Now sketching the smile shape with a curved stroke path and small corner tick marks for expression, scaling considerations for raster output.

Designing the blush ellipse with subtle hatch lines inside it, then starting on the frill gradient definition...

I'm designing a second, paler frill variant with a more slender wavy shape and a gradient from rose to near-white, adjusting stroke widths for the scaled-up 128px canvas. Now I'm starting to write the final TypeScript module, importing three.js and the helper utilities for randomness, limb building, painting, and spot patterns.

Still writing build logic...

Then head etc. I'm defining a height function for the dorsal fin using interpolated keyframes along the z-axis, with a generic ramp helper for smoothing between points. I'm computing the fin's start and end t-values along the spine, making sure the end comes after the root, then building the membrane geometry starting from a trunk line offset.

For the ventral fin I'm doing the same tapering height approach, finding closest-t points on the spine to bound the fin's extent near the tail. But I'm catching a problem: near the tail the body floor is very low, so the ventral fin's downward extension would poke below the floor -- I need to check how the tail's bottom contour rises to avoid that clipping issue.

Skipping the ventral fin entirely and instead curving the tail upward progressively toward the tip feels like the better fix—a gentle lift function that makes the tail curl slightly, giving it a cute chibi look without worrying about floor clipping.

Now I'm working out the hind foot toe angles—computing the azimuth for each side so the toes point backward-outward, matching how axolotl hind feet naturally splay.

Setting front hand finger spread at 70° and hind foot toe spread at 90°, with digit lengths and radii tuned per limb. I'm also positioning the hind leg lower segment relative to the knee, sizing the palm sphere, and working out the gill hit positions using azimuth/elevation angles mirrored by side.

Working out the fan-tuning gill directions for top and mid segments, checking tip heights against head scale, and adjusting x-spread since the mid gills come out too wide compared to the chibi head size.

I'm also placing the collar sphere and checking the stick/cards helper functions take the right parameters before writing the final code, including nostril positions on the snout.
